title: Distributed compute fundamentals
summary: How analytical engines split work across machines, why shuffles and skew dominate performance, and which engine fits which workload.

blocks.text: 5.1 From one machine to many

A single modern server with dozens of cores, hundreds of GB of RAM and fast NVMe disks can process hundreds of GB of columnar data quickly. Distribution is needed when data or concurrency outgrow that, and it has a price: coordination, network transfer and partial failures. A good architect asks first whether the workload really needs a cluster.

Distributed analytical engines share one idea: split data into **partitions**, run the same operation on each partition in parallel (**data parallelism**), and move data between machines only when an operation needs rows with the same key together.
5.2 Shared-nothing, MPP and separated storage

**MPP** (massively parallel processing) describes execution: a query is split into fragments that run in parallel on many nodes. **Shared-nothing** describes resources: each node owns its CPU, memory and a slice of the data on local disks. Classic warehouses (Teradata, early Redshift, Greenplum) combined both: data was hash-distributed across nodes, and each node scanned its own slice.

Shared-nothing scales well but couples storage and compute. Adding nodes means redistributing data; idle compute still has to stay up to keep the data online; and two workloads cannot get separate compute over the same data without copying it. Cloud-native designs therefore **separate storage and compute**: data lives on object storage, and independent compute clusters read it on demand, with local SSD caches to recover most of the locality.

Data lives
Scaling

blocks.text: Separated storage and compute is what makes *workload isolation* cheap: the ETL cluster, the BI cluster and the data science cluster read the same tables without competing for CPU. That property drives much of the cloud warehouse and lakehouse design in chapters 26 and 42.
5.3 Stages and shuffles

Operations that work row by row (filter, project, simple functions) run on each partition independently. Operations that need all rows with the same key together (`GROUP BY`, joins, `DISTINCT`, window functions with `PARTITION BY`) force a **shuffle**: every task hashes each row's key and sends it over the network to the task responsible for that key. A shuffle ends a stage; the next stage starts on the redistributed data.

blocks.title: A GROUP BY in a distributed engine
blocks.caption: Partial aggregation before the shuffle reduces how much data crosses the network.

blocks.text: Shuffles are usually the most expensive part of a distributed query: they serialize data, write it (in Spark, to local disk), send it across the network and read it back. Reading a query plan is largely about finding the shuffles (`Exchange` nodes in Spark plans) and asking whether each one is necessary.
5.4 Join strategies

head: Strategy
How it works
Good when
Risk
rows: Send the small table to every task; build a hash table; stream the big table
One side is small (MB to low hundreds of MB)
Driver/executor memory errors if the small side is not small
Shuffle both sides by key; build a hash table per partition from the smaller side
Smaller side too big to broadcast but each partition fits in memory
Shuffle both sides by key, sort each partition, merge
Both sides large; Spark's default for big equi-joins

blocks.text: Spark chooses broadcast automatically when a side's estimated size is under `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default), and Adaptive Query Execution can switch to a broadcast at runtime once actual sizes are known. You can also hint it.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: forcing a broadcast of a dimension
blocks.text:
SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(c) */
       c.country_name,
       sum(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM   sales.orders o
JOIN   ref.countries c
  ON   o.country_code = c.country_code
GROUP  BY c.country_name;

Bad statistics produce bad join choices. A filtered table that the optimizer thinks is 5 GB may be broadcast-eligible; a table it thinks is tiny may actually be huge and crash executors when broadcast. Keep table statistics current and check the physical plan of critical jobs.
5.5 Skew and spill

**Skew** means some keys have far more rows than others. After a shuffle, the task that owns the hot key (a `NULL` customer id, a giant marketplace seller, a default country) gets most of the data. The stage runs as slowly as its slowest task, so one straggler can take an hour while 199 others finished in a minute.

items: **Detect**: in the Spark UI, compare max and median task duration and shuffle read size in a stage. A ratio above roughly 10x signals skew.
**Filter or split hot values**: handle `NULL` keys separately; they never match an equi-join anyway.
**Adaptive skew handling**: Spark AQE can split oversized shuffle partitions in sort-merge joins when skew join handling is enabled.
**Salting**: append a random suffix (0..N-1) to the hot key on the big side and replicate the small side N times, so one key spreads over N tasks.
**Broadcast**: if the other side is small, a broadcast join avoids shuffling the skewed side at all.

blocks.text: **Spill** happens when a task's data for a sort, aggregation or hash table does not fit in its memory, so the engine writes intermediate data to local disk and reads it back. Spill keeps the job alive but can make it many times slower. Causes are too few shuffle partitions (the Spark default of 200 is often wrong for large data), skew, or undersized executors. Warehouses report the same thing as *bytes spilled to local/remote storage* in query profiles.

blocks.title: A nightly job stuck at 199/200
blocks.text: A Spark job joining 2 billion orders with 50 million customers ran 3 hours, with one task taking 2.5 of them.
items: The shuffle read for that task was 80 GB versus a median of 400 MB: orders with `customer_id IS NULL` from guest checkouts.
Guest orders were split out and unioned back after the join, since they cannot match anyway.
With AQE enabled and shuffle partitions raised for the remaining data, the job ran in 25 minutes.

blocks.text: Many platforms combine several: Spark or a warehouse for heavy transformation, Trino or the warehouse for interactive queries, DuckDB for development and tests. Open table formats make this practical, because each engine reads the same tables (chapter 21).

blocks.title: Diagnose a slow join
blocks.text: A daily job joins a 3 TB clickstream table with a 400 MB product table and a 900 GB sessions table, then aggregates by product category. It takes 4 hours and spills heavily. Describe what you would look for in the plan and the UI, which join strategies you expect for each join, and three changes you would try in order.
hints: Is the 400 MB table broadcastable with your executor memory?
Check whether a few session ids or products dominate the shuffle.

items: MPP describes parallel execution; shared-nothing describes resource ownership; modern engines separate storage and compute.
Shuffles redistribute rows by key and are usually the dominant cost; partial aggregation reduces them.
Broadcast joins avoid shuffling the big side; sort-merge is the default for two large inputs.
Skew makes one task the bottleneck; fix with null handling, AQE, salting or broadcast.
Spill to disk signals too little memory per task: more partitions, less skew or bigger executors.

blocks.q: Which operation does NOT require a shuffle on its own?
blocks.explain: A filter works on each partition independently. Grouping, distinct counting and sort-merge joins need rows with the same key on the same task.

blocks.q: A stage has 200 tasks: 199 finish in about 1 minute, one runs for 50 minutes with a huge shuffle read. What is the most likely cause?
options: Key skew sends most rows to one task
The cluster has too few nodes
The driver is out of memory
blocks.explain: One task with a far larger shuffle read than the median is the signature of skew. More nodes would not help because the hot key still lands on one task.

blocks.q: What is the main benefit of separating storage from compute?
options: Data no longer needs to be partitioned
Queries no longer need the network
Independent compute clusters can scale and serve different workloads over the same data
blocks.explain: Separation lets compute be resized, paused and isolated per workload while storage stays shared. It actually adds network reads (mitigated by caches) and does not remove shuffles.

blocks.q: When is a broadcast hash join a poor choice?
options: When the query is an equi-join
When the smaller side is many GB and does not fit in each executor's memory
When the dimension table is 2 MB
When the join key is skewed on the large side
blocks.explain: Broadcasting copies the small side to every executor, which fails or thrashes if it is large. With a tiny side and skewed big side, broadcast is actually a good fix.
